findings.body:
Removing the `ALLOWED_HOSTS` guard lets `deliver()` POST the event to any customer-supplied URL via `urllib.request.urlopen`. A value such as `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/` or `http://127.0.0.1:8080/` is fetched from this process, and `urlopen` follows redirects by default, so this is SSRF against cloud metadata, loopback, and private networks.

Keep supporting customer endpoints, but validate before `Request`: require `https`, reject loopback/link-local/private IPs after DNS resolution, and re-check the target on every redirect.

summary:
I'd recommend not merging until the SSRF at `webhooks.py:6` is closed.

`deliver()` now posts the event body to whatever `url` the caller supplies. The only control that previously constrained that host (`ALLOWED_HOSTS` plus the `urlsplit` check) is gone, and `urllib.request.urlopen` still follows redirects and accepts non-HTTPS schemes. A customer-controlled value such as `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/` or `http://127.0.0.1:8080/` is fetched from this process, which can reach link-local metadata, loopback, and private networks and leak the POSTed event.

Customer-owned endpoints are a reasonable product goal. They need an explicit URL policy (HTTPS, public addresses after DNS resolution, re-validate redirects) in front of `Request`/`urlopen`, not an unrestricted fetch.

**Recommendation:** request-changes

verification.reason: The base `deliver()` blocked hosts outside `ALLOWED_HOSTS`; head removes that check and POSTs the customer-supplied URL with `urllib.request.urlopen`, which follows redirects and has no scheme/host/IP validation—classic SSRF to metadata/loopback/private nets. Critical severity is appropriate.
